summary: Describes a structure for representing trust anchor information. A trust anchor is an authoritative entity represented by a public key plus data that limits what it is trusted for. It meets the format needs set out in the trust anchor management requirements. It is a Proposed Standard.

plainLanguage.summary: A trust anchor is the public key a system trusts to start from, the root of the chain that leads to a website's certificate. This document gives that key a standard packed format, so a trust anchor can be sent from one system to another, and so limits can be attached to it, such as which names it is allowed to vouch for.

questions: what is a trust anchor list
subtitle: A standard, compact record of a trust anchor: its public key plus limits on what it is trusted to vouch for.

tldr.problem: Trust anchors are needed to validate certification paths, but there was no standard format for representing trust anchor information.
tldr.mechanism: The TrustAnchorInfo structure, written in ASN.1, holds the public key, a key identifier, an optional title and optional certification path controls. A TrustAnchorList can hold many anchors.
tldr.outcome: Trust anchors can be exchanged in a compact form, and constraints can be attached without breaking a certificate's signature. The RFC is a Proposed Standard.

today: RFC 5914 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata records no obsoleting or updating document, so it remains the standard format for trust anchor information, alongside the X.509 certificate profile in RFC 5280.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Trust anchors are widely used to verify digital signatures and validate certification paths. They are required when validating certification paths. Though widely used, there is no standard format for representing trust anchor information.

This document describes the TrustAnchorInfo structure. The structure is intended to satisfy the format-related requirements expressed in Trust Anchor Management Requirements, and is expressed using ASN.1. It can provide a more compact alternative to X.509 certificates for exchanging trust anchor information, and it provides a means of associating additional or alternative constraints with certificates without breaking the signature on the certificate.
sections.plainLanguage: Every system that checks certificates needs at least one key it believes in, and usually a list of them. There was no agreed way to write that list down, so different systems did it differently. This document defines one way, in ASN.1, the notation used to describe structured data in X.509 certificates.

sections.title: The TrustAnchorInfo Structure
sections.content:
The TrustAnchorInfo structure is a SEQUENCE with a version that defaults to v1, a mandatory pubKey of type SubjectPublicKeyInfo, a mandatory keyId, and then optional fields: a title, a set of certification path controls, extensions, and a language tag for the title.

The version identifies the version of TrustAnchorInfo. Future updates to the document may include changes to the structure, in which case the version number should be incremented, but the default value v1 cannot be changed.

The pubKey field identifies the public key and algorithm associated with the trust anchor using the SubjectPublicKeyInfo structure. That structure contains the algorithm identifier followed by the public key itself. The algorithm field is an AlgorithmIdentifier, which contains an object identifier and optional parameters. The object identifier names the public key algorithm and indicates the syntax of the parameters, if present, as well as the format of the public key. The public key is encoded as a BIT STRING. The keyId field contains the public key identifier of the trust anchor public key.

The title is OPTIONAL, and when present provides a human-readable name for the trust anchor. The text is encoded in UTF-8, which accommodates most of the world's writing systems. The title language tag field identifies the language used to express the title; when that field is absent, English is used, and the value should be a language tag as described in BCP 47. The title is a UTF8String with a size of 1 to 64 characters.
sections.plainLanguage: The record has three things that are always there: a version number, the public key itself, and an identifier for that key. Then it can carry a name for people to read, a set of limits on what the key may vouch for, extra extension fields, and the language the name is written in. The name is at most 64 characters and defaults to English.

sections.title: Certification Path Controls
sections.content:
The certPath field is OPTIONAL. When it is present, it provides the controls needed to initialize an X.509 certification path validation algorithm implementation. When absent, the trust anchor cannot be used to validate the signature on an X.509 certificate.

The taName field provides the X.500 distinguished name associated with the trust anchor, and this distinguished name is used to construct and validate an X.509 certification path. The name MUST NOT be an empty sequence. The optional certificate field provides an X.509 certificate, which can be used in some environments to represent the trust anchor in certification path development and validation. If the certificate is present, the subject name in it MUST exactly match the distinguished name in taName, the public key MUST exactly match the public key in pubKey, and the subjectKeyIdentifier extension, if present, MUST exactly match the key identifier in keyId.

Constraints defined in the policySet, policyFlags, nameConstr, pathLenConstraint and exts fields replace values contained in a certificate, or provide values for extensions not present in the certificate. Values defined in these TrustAnchorInfo fields are always enforced. Extensions included in a certificate are enforced only if there is no corresponding value in the TrustAnchorInfo.

The policySet is OPTIONAL and contains a sequence of certificate policy identifiers to be provided as inputs to the certification path validation algorithm. When absent, the special value any-policy is provided as the input. The policyFlags field is OPTIONAL and carries three Boolean values: inhibitPolicyMapping, requireExplicitPolicy and inhibitAnyPolicy. When absent, the input is the most liberal setting for these flags. The inhibitPolicyMapping bit indicates whether policy mapping is allowed in the certification path. The requireExplicitPolicy bit indicates whether the certification path must be valid for at least one of the certificate policies in the policySet, and this bit must be set to FALSE if policySet is absent. The inhibitAnyPolicy bit indicates whether the special anyPolicy policy identifier, with the value { 2 5 29 32 0 }, is considered an explicit match for other certificate policies.

The nameConstr field is OPTIONAL and has the same syntax and semantics as the Name Constraints certificate extension, which includes a list of permitted names and a list of excluded names. When present, constraints are provided on names, including alternative names, that might appear in subsequent X.509 certificates in a certification path. When absent, the permitted subtrees are unbounded and the excluded subtrees are empty. The pathLenConstraint field gives the maximum number of non-self-issued intermediate certificates that may follow this certificate in a valid certification path. A value of zero indicates that no non-self-issued intermediate certification authority certificates may follow. Where pathLenConstraint does not appear, no limit is imposed.

An application validating a certification path should not ignore these limitations, but it can impose additional limitations to ensure the validated path is appropriate for its context. As input to the validation algorithm, an application may provide a subset of the policies, set any of the flags to TRUE if appropriate, provide a subset of the permitted names, provide additional excluded names, or provide a smaller value for pathLenConstraint.
sections.plainLanguage: These are the limits on what the trust anchor may vouch for. There is a name the anchor is known by, a list of certificate policies that are acceptable, three switches about how policies may be mapped along the chain, a list of names that are permitted or forbidden below the anchor, and a limit on how many intermediate certificates may sit between the anchor and the end certificate. An application is allowed to tighten any of these, but should not loosen them.

sections.title: Extensions
sections.content: The exts field is OPTIONAL. When present, it can be used to associate additional information with the trust anchor using the standard Extensions structure. Extensions that are anticipated to be widely used have been included in the CertPathControls structure to avoid the overhead associated with use of the Extensions structure. To avoid duplication with the CertPathControls field, the following types of extensions MUST NOT appear in the exts field and are ignored if they do: id-ce-certificatePolicies, id-ce-policyConstraints, id-ce-inhibitAnyPolicy, or id-ce-nameConstraints.
sections.plainLanguage: Anything else the trust anchor needs to carry goes in a standard extensions field, the same one certificates use. The four extensions that already have a home in the controls structure are not allowed here, so there is only one place to look for each value.

sections.title: Trust Anchor Lists
sections.content:
TrustAnchorInfo allows for the representation of a single trust anchor. In many cases it is convenient to represent a collection of trust anchors, so the TrustAnchorList structure is defined for this purpose. TrustAnchorList is a sequence of one or more TrustAnchorChoice objects, and TrustAnchorChoice provides three options for representing a trust anchor.

The certificate option allows for the use of a certificate with no additional associated constraints. The tbsCert option allows for associating constraints by removing a signature on a certificate and changing the extensions field. The taInfo option allows for use of the TrustAnchorInfo structure defined in this document.

The TrustAnchorList structure can be protected using the SignedData structure defined in the Cryptographic Message Syntax. The id-ct-trustAnchorList object identifier has been defined to represent TrustAnchorList payloads with CMS structures.
sections.plainLanguage: A list holds one or more trust anchors, and each entry can be written in one of three ways: as a plain certificate, as a certificate with its signature removed so that extra constraints can be added without invalidating it, or as the compact TrustAnchorInfo record this document defines. A whole list can be signed with CMS so that receivers know it has not been altered.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Compromise of a trust anchor private key permits unauthorized parties to masquerade as the trust anchor, with potentially severe consequences. Where trust-anchor-based constraints are enforced, the unauthorized holder of the trust anchor private key will be limited by the certification path controls associated with the trust anchor, as expressed in the certPath and exts fields. For example, name constraints in the trust anchor will determine the name space that will be accepted in certificates that are validated using the compromised trust anchor. Reliance on an inappropriate or incorrect trust anchor public key has similar potentially severe consequences.

The compromise of a certificate authority's private key leads to the same type of problems as the compromise of a trust anchor private key. The unauthorized holder of the certificate authority private key will be limited by the certification path controls associated with the trust anchor, as expressed in the certPath field or as an extension.

Usage of a certificate independent of the TrustAnchorInfo structure that envelopes it must be carefully managed to avoid violating constraints expressed in the TrustAnchorInfo. When enveloping a certificate in a TrustAnchorInfo structure, values included in the certificate should be evaluated to ensure there is no confusion or conflict with values in the TrustAnchorInfo structure.
sections.plainLanguage: If the private key behind a trust anchor is stolen, the thief can pretend to be that anchor. The limits stored alongside the anchor are what still stand in the way, because they restrict which names the thief can get certificates for. The same applies to a stolen certificate authority key. And if a certificate is wrapped inside a TrustAnchorInfo record, the two have to be checked for conflicting values.
